title: "SLAM"

term: "SLAM"

## Simple explanation

SLAM lets a robot build a map of an unfamiliar place while estimating
where it is in that map. The two problems depend on each other: a better
position estimate improves the map, and a better map helps locate the robot.

## Technical explanation

Simultaneous localization and mapping estimates a trajectory and map from
noisy sensor measurements, such as camera images, lidar scans, or odometry.
Methods include filtering and graph-based optimization. Loop closure
recognizes revisited places and can correct accumulated drift.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

SLAM supports mobile robots, autonomous vehicles, and augmented reality
systems operating without a complete prebuilt map. Sensor calibration,
environmental ambiguity, compute limits, and real-time reliability are
important engineering concerns.

## How it works

The system extracts or tracks observations, estimates motion between
measurements, and adds constraints to a map or pose graph. Optimization
reconciles these constraints over time. Sensor fusion can combine camera,
inertial, wheel, or range data.

## Practical example

A mobile robot can use lidar and wheel odometry to estimate movement while
mapping corridor geometry. When it recognizes a previously visited area,
loop closure can reduce drift in the estimated route and map.

## Common misconceptions

- SLAM does not produce a perfect map or exact location; estimates have
  uncertainty and may drift.
- A map built by one sensor or environment may not work unchanged in a
  different environment.
